# the contributor audit: thin laws, common lifts, and vanishing-mass obstructions


The statements do not prove continuity of depth under weak convergence
or resolve the general mixed-integer inequality.

## Normalized thin convex measures and compatible ball lifts

I read all six sections of
`candidate b9e8ea5c75ef1e0e`.
The weak-closure argument uses lower Portmanteau on open source
neighborhoods and upper Portmanteau on the closed target neighborhood
in the correct direction. Borell's stated parameter conversion uses
the affine support dimension q: a 1/m-concave measure has density
exponent 1/(m-q) when q<m. The finite exponent is not applied at q=m.

The boundedness proof for positive concave density roots is valid:
midpoints with a fixed positive interior ball give fixed-radius balls
with a uniform positive density lower bound. Escaping support points
would give infinite total mass; unbounded root values would already
give arbitrarily large mass on one such ball. The compact concave
upper-semicontinuous extension changes no full-q-dimensional measure.

The common-weight ball lift has exactly the specified unnormalized
mass by Fubini and is convex by radius concavity. The q=m uniform case
correctly retains its actual volume, and an optional extra height
coordinate is explicitly identified as a dimension increase. The
lengths 1,2,1 example genuinely disproves all equal-volume convex lifts
under independent probability normalization, by BM equality; common
relative masses repair that example exactly as stated.

The simultaneous Schwarz construction uses ONE projection and ONE
normalization constant, so sectional BM preserves every anchored
Minkowski inclusion. Its projection identities control precisely those
cap normals in the retained subspace. It makes no assertion about
discarded normal components. In the thin-limit construction, full
projected support supplies a uniform projection ball; averaging it
with a maximum-radius point gives the stated bound on all lifted
radii. Volume continuity, rotational symmetry and closure of the
interior give a unique full-dimensional limiting lift, justifying
whole-sequence convergence.

The direct cross-measure argument in Section 6 has the correct exponent.
The small-ball radii are optimized under their weighted-sum constraint;
Jensen gives the displayed maximum S^(1-q/m), attained at a_i=b_i/S.
This proves root-density concavity for ALL finite anchored combinations.
Interior continuity and convex closure supply the full boundary
inclusions. Conversely, cylinders in the compatible lifts and ordinary
BM give the original cross-measure inequality. Common normalization is
retained throughout. The q=m target-density maximum condition and its
optional additional-height realization are also correct.

This is an exact common-support representation and projection theorem.
It does not identify differently oriented original support laws with
their common projections, and it does not recover prelimit depths from
weak convergence.

## Vanishing coarse mass, full hulls, and a face obstruction

I read all seven sections of
`candidate e306d42187c98e53` and
recomputed its principal geometric and mass identities independently.
The two thin triangles have area 2epsilon each and contain the two
orthogonal limiting segments. Their hull limit is the full tetrahedron
of volume 2/3. The stated fixed normalization has a unit inner ball.
Each original triangle's exact maximal depth is 4/9, and finite
integer tilts isolate its caps from the other base, giving exact mixed
maximum 2/9. The weak limit has two one-dimensional non-atomic laws,
whose median depths are 1/4 after the equal mixture weights. The fixed
halfspace in (8) has exactly the claimed boundary-mass jump.

The fine-grid example samples all vertices. Its two exact weighted
masses are 2/ell+1/ell^3 and 2/ell. The uniform cap error divided by
their total tends to zero, and the explicit rounded first-triangle
centroid loses only O(1/ell). Thus the fine maximal depths also tend
to 2/9; no weak-depth continuity assertion is used to obtain this.

A full-dimensional hull has full-dimensional fibers over every interior
projection point, so all-zero coarse fiber volumes force a hollow
projection. In rank one a fixed lattice-convex full-rank support is
therefore exactly two adjacent bases. The prelimit consequence now
explicitly keeps that SAME support; the abstract limit does not imply
it for an unspecified varying support.

The rank-two affine-box example is convex and is exactly the hull of
its integer vertex fibers. Its three vertex masses are 8epsilon^2,
its three midpoint masses are 2epsilon(1+epsilon)^2, and subtraction
gives M-2 M_edge=2epsilon(1-epsilon)^2>0. The limiting hull is full
dimensional although every coarse integer fiber has zero full volume.
This refutes only an automatic half-mass supporting face; it is not an
OC counterexample or a refutation of all possible face allocations.
note: Mathematical discussion retained to expose corrections and limitations. This is not a verification run, accepted premise, or approval of the revised submission. Association follows explicit source-document references, not an inferred dependency.
